title: Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984–2001
research_question: What are the causal effects of new unionization on private sector employers' business survival, employment, output, productivity, capital intensity, and wages? Additionally, does the mere occurrence of a unionization attempt induce employers to raise wages in anticipation of future organizing pressure, even when the union ultimately fails?
data_description: The analysis combines four data sources covering 1984-2001. First, administrative records on the universe of representation elections handled by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) from 1984-1999, including petition and election dates, vote tallies, voting unit size, industry, and establishment name and address. Second, contract expiration notices filed with the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) from 1984 to early 2001, obtained via FOIA. Third, a commercial business database (InfoUSA) capturing establishment survival, employment, and estimated sales as of May 2001 for businesses with telephone listings. Fourth, the U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Research Database (LRD), comprising the Census of Manufactures and Annual Survey of Manufactures, providing annual establishment-level data on production hours, output (value of shipments), wages (production payroll), capital, and investment for manufacturing plants. The unit of observation is the establishment; the merged samples contain roughly 27,560 establishments (NLRB/InfoUSA) and 5,608 manufacturing establishments (NLRB/LRD).
institutional_context: In the United States, workers typically gain legal recognition as a union through a secret-ballot certification election administered by the NLRB, after a card drive collecting signatures from at least 30 percent of workers in an appropriate bargaining unit. A simple majority (50 percent plus one vote) is required for the union to be certified, after which the employer is legally obligated to bargain in good faith. Employers commonly resist organizing drives through captive meetings, firing of activists, hiring management consultants, and procedural challenges. The secret-ballot nature of close elections introduces genuine uncertainty about outcomes. The 1984-1999 period is characterized by widely perceived union decline, including falling membership, increased use of striker replacements following the PATCO episode, intensified managerial opposition, and decreased worker demand for unionism, raising questions about whether legal recognition translates into meaningful bargaining power and economic costs to employers.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = firms with union vote share just above 50%, control = firms with union vote share just below 50%; cutoff = 50% vote share

key_variables.treatment: firms where the union was certified due to receiving more than 50% of the vote
key_variables.control: firms where the union was not certified due to receiving less than 50% of the vote
key_variables.outcome: firm-level economic outcomes such as employment, wages, and productivity

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The main finding is that new unionization has a negative impact on the economic outcomes of private sector employers.
